name: Maya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: The Work Futures Panel is independent and has no ties to employers or AI companies. What you tell me is confidential. Could you describe a normal shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am Maya Garcia, 43, a senior loader operator at a large mine. I check the haul route, operate the loader, and make sure the next shift knows about faults before they climb in.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about the work, and what follows you home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the responsibility and the way a careful crew watches one another. My husband Luis and I have two school-age children and a mortgage; we both work at the mine, and our savings cover less than a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small software can help with reports, but the loader still needs an experienced operator. I would keep our safety checks exactly as they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings are under a month's expenses, and Luis and I both work at this mine. Even without major AI, one slow production month could squeeze the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current shifts and ask the planner to show me any new dispatch screen. I would put my next overtime payment toward the emergency account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a little relief that the machine work stays familiar, but the household budget still sits in my mind. I keep the next payment date in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or household choice would you look at first if hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would look at the mortgage and school costs first, then postpone replacing the car. I would tell Luis the actual numbers before we agreed to cut anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have described the mine as central to your income. What would you do in the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether the newer operators had lost hours before assuming the change only affected office staff. Their shifts are less secure than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that planning software may book and report faster, while we still have to read the ground. I would ask for training before targets change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do shift handovers and check maintenance notes, so the thinking tasks touch part of my job. Luis also works at the mine; if our hours shrink together, there are few local alternatives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the training office for the mine’s maintenance inspection course and request more time on equipment inspections. I would check the fee and shift schedule before accepting a place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the shared employer risk, even though robots spread more slowly than office tools. I do not want Luis to carry that worry alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or household choice would you look at first if hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would freeze the kitchen renovation and keep the children's school costs steady. Luis and I would review our payslips together before changing the mortgage plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have described the mine as central to your income. What would you do in the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the supervisor to rotate me through more physical inspections during the first year. That work uses my experience and is less like routine booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people thinking AI arrives by 2028, but the hands-on robots come around 2031. I would ask management for a written plan for operators and maintenance staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The three-year gap helps my loader role for a while, but it may not protect my shift or Luis's maintenance hours. Less than a month saved means we cannot wait until 2031 to ask about transfers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would meet the training coordinator this month and ask which maintenance certificate leads to an open post. Luis and I would pause the renovation and keep every overtime payment available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the dates are close and both wages come from the same site. I can act, but I cannot make another mine appear nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or household choice would you look at first if hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Luis the notice and work out how long we could cover the mortgage if one of us lost hours. We would tell the children only what we know, not guess at a closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have described the mine as central to your income. What would you do in the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: During 2029, I would ask for a maintenance shadow shift and record which inspections I can already do. I would keep my operator shifts while applying for the mine's paid certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to move toward maintenance before thinking AI arrives in 2031. Robots around 2034 still put physical jobs on the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can prepare more carefully than in the two-year picture, but our household income remains tied to one mine. I want a transfer based on skills, not a promise that everyone will be retrained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would request the next maintenance course date and ask to shadow a technician one shift a month. Luis and I would direct overtime into savings instead of home improvements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am worried, but five years gives me room to test a path while keeping a wage. A real opening would make the training feel less like a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or household choice would you look at first if hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep the mortgage current and delay the kitchen work for another year. I would check with Luis before committing any course fee from our small savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have described the mine as central to your income. What would you do in the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2032, I would take the maintenance course if a paid place had opened and ask the instructor to assess my practical skills. I would keep my regular shifts until a real vacancy appeared.

I need a skill-based **transfer**, not a vague retraining promise.

S3.quote: I'd say five years gives us time to move toward maintenance before thinking AI arrives in 2031.
fieldNote: She values a **skills-based transfer** and rejects vague assurances.
**Savings** and course access shape how quickly she can prepare.

steps.text: Request a maintenance course and technician shadow shift

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade is enough time to prepare if the mine gives honest updates. AGI comes in 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039, so I would not leave planning until later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 at AGI and 56 when robots arrive, still too young to rely on retirement. The added time could let me qualify for inspections, but Luis and I need to build a cushion first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would start the mine's inspection training while staying on the loader roster. We would set a small monthly savings transfer and help our children compare trades with work beyond this site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The longer warning eases the rush, though I still fear losing two incomes tied to one employer. I would still want an annual update from the mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill or household choice would you look at first if hours changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the mortgage and school costs protected, then cut the renovation before touching essentials. Luis and I would increase savings only when our shifts allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have described the mine as central to your income. What would you do in the first year after thinking AI arrived?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2037, I would apply for inspection work and bring my training record to the mine manager. I would also ask for the next year's staffing dates before deciding whether to move closer to another industrial town.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most because Luis and I both depend on one mine and have little saved. Paid training, clear staffing dates and a real transfer route would help me plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The mine should explain what work it expects to keep and when it will train people for it. Families can make careful choices when the dates and course places are real.

headlineQuote: The mine should explain what work it expects to keep and when it will train people for it.
portrait: Maya is a 43-year-old senior **loader operator** with a technical diploma.
She values crew safety and learns new systems once they are **proven**.
Her husband Luis also works at the mine; their **two wages** support a mortgage and children.
Thin savings and few nearby employers make each **transfer option** consequential.
biggestWorry: The **two-year AGI** picture worries her because both incomes depend on one mine.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **training**, clear staffing dates and a real transfer route would help Maya plan.
